analysis.one_liner: Restores federal Clean Water Act protection to all U.S. waters, overturning two Supreme Court rulings.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or vote, after being referred on April 22, 2010.
analysis.plain_summary: Two Supreme Court decisions narrowed which waters the Clean Water Act covers, leaving many streams and wetlands without federal protection. This bill rewrote the law's key definition, replacing 'navigable waters' with 'waters of the United States' so small streams, wetlands, and prairie potholes that feed drinking water supplies were covered again. It excluded existing farm cropland and waste treatment systems to limit the reach. The bill was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its water subcommittee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water sourced from small streams and wetlands: the bill's findings state that such source areas supply drinking water systems serving more than 117 million people. Also anglers, boaters, and communities whose lakes and rivers depend on upstream headwaters staying clean.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose drinking water comes from small streams

how_it_helps.text: Replaces 'navigable waters' with 'waters of the United States' throughout the Clean Water Act, restoring the scope of federal jurisdiction that existed before the 2001 SWANCC and 2006 Rapanos Supreme Court decisions.
Brings intermittent streams, wetlands, prairie potholes, mudflats, and adjacent waters back under Clean Water Act protection, closing the gap left for geographically isolated and intrastate waters.
Protects headwater streams that feed drinking water supplies serving more than 117 million people, according to the bill's congressional findings.

analysis.who_pays: Landowners, developers, and farmers who would need federal permits before filling or discharging into newly covered waters. Existing prior converted cropland and documented waste treatment systems are excluded, but other wetlands and new treatment systems built in covered waters would face permitting.

drawbacks.text: The expanded definition reaches intermittent streams, wetlands, sloughs, prairie potholes, and natural ponds, which would subject more construction, farming, and land-use decisions to federal permitting requirements and their costs and delays.

The farm carve-out is narrow: only cropland converted before December 23, 1985 is excluded, and EPA, not the Agriculture Department, gets final say over whether land qualifies as prior converted cropland, leaving other farm wetlands regulated.

While existing documented waste treatment systems are grandfathered, no new waste treatment system may be created in or by impounding waters of the United States, limiting how municipalities can site treatment facilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: broader water protection means more federal permitting that can slow construction and farming, and the bill tries to blunt that with the cropland and treatment-system carve-outs. For anyone whose drinking water or recreational waters depend on small upstream streams, the protective value is large; the permit burden falls mainly on those who would discharge or fill those waters. The main design weakness is that a definition this broad depends on regulators drawing the lines case by case, which is exactly the uncertainty opponents cited.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then its Water Resources and Environment subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Oberstar introduced the bill on April 21, 2010, with Reps. Dingell and Ehlers joining as cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it stayed for the rest of the 111th Congress.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landowners, developers, and farm and industry groups that would have faced federal permitting under the broader water definition; they keep the narrower post-2006 jurisdiction. People relying on streams and wetlands for drinking water gain nothing, since the protections never took effect.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor — but with only two cosponsors in the whole House and no recorded vote, the partisan shape of the deadlock was never tested.

industries.note: Filling wetlands and building across small streams would require Clean Water Act permits under the broader definition. Their interest in narrower jurisdiction runs against the public's interest in clean water and protected drinking water sources.

The bill explicitly excludes prior converted cropland, shielding most drained farm fields from the new jurisdiction, but other farm wetlands, prairie potholes, and intermittent streams on farmland would be covered, and EPA rather than USDA gets the final call. Most existing farm drainage is exempted; expansions into wetter ground are not.
Discharges and fills into previously unregulated streams, wetlands, and ponds would need permits. The industry benefits from the narrower post-Rapanos jurisdiction the bill would have reversed.

Existing documented treatment systems are grandfathered even if built in or by impounding covered waters, but the bill bars any new treatment system from being created in such waters, constraining how towns can site future facilities.

Cleaner streams and protected wetlands support fishing, boating, and water-based tourism, which the bill's findings say generate billions in income annually. This interest moves with the public's interest in clean water.
